introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 3 (0790), Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section (Section One: Logic; Section Two: Philosophical Problems). Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion, as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Dissertation : réponse modèle (introduction avec problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse, conclusion, environ 600 à 700 mots), structurée selon les critères de la page de garde (cohérence, problématique, thèse-antithèse-synthèse-conclusion). La page de garde de 2024 n'imprime pas de barème par partie : aucun partage de points n'est inventé. Auteurs cités dans leurs positions connues, sans citation littérale, sans titre d'ouvrage détaillé, sans date ni numéro de page.

Q6 : question religieuse ; le corrigé expose les positions et leurs raisons sans prendre parti de croyance, et conclut sur l'argument le mieux étayé (la critique de l'existence tirée du seul concept). Positions attribuées de façon générale et prudente : Anselme (définition, existence dans l'entendement puis dans la réalité, existence nécessaire ; la formule est la citation imprimée dans le sujet), Gaunilo (l'île parfaite) et réponse d'Anselme, Thomas d'Aquin (évident en soi, non évident pour nous), Descartes, Leibniz (possibilité du concept), Hume, Kant (l'existence n'est pas un prédicat réel, exemple de cent pièces), Plantinga (versions modales). Aucun titre d'ouvrage, date ni numéro de chapitre.

Numérotation : le sujet imprime « 3. », « 4. », « 5. », « 6. » ; les questions 1 et 2 n'ont pas de numéro lisible (la question 1 est annoncée par le passage de lecture, la question 2 par un point isolé devant « (a) »). Numéros déduits de la suite 1 à 6 ; la section Logic compte donc trois questions, la section Philosophical Problems trois.

Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section » (quatre questions au total, deux par section). Section One (Logic) : questions 1 à 3 ; Section Two (Philosophical Problems) : questions 4 à 6. `regles_choix` porte une règle `parmi 2 sur 3` par section ; la règle « 4 en tout » est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : le corrigé est une réponse modèle rédigée ; la logique est recalculée avec Python (itertools, modèles d'ensembles), la philosophie est donnée de mémoire (auteurs et positions de l'histoire établie de la philosophie, sans citation littérale, titre d'ouvrage, date ni numéro de page). À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné de 4 pages (page de garde, Section One pages 2 et 3, Section Two page 4) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo, sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024, Philosophy, Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), Subject Code 0790, trois heures.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**6.** "God is that than which nothing greater can be thought". Evaluate this assertion by St. Anselm.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** St. Anselm of Canterbury, a medieval Benedictine theologian, defines God as "that than which nothing greater can be thought" and uses this definition to argue that God **must exist**. The argument, later called the **ontological argument**, is meant to be a proof from the very idea of God, without any appeal to experience of the world. To evaluate the assertion is to ask two questions: is the definition acceptable and coherent, and does it really establish the existence of God? The problem is whether reasoning from a concept can reach a reality.

**Thesis: the assertion is a sound definition and an argument of real force.**

- *The argument.* Even the person who denies God understands the phrase "that than which nothing greater can be thought", so such a being **exists in the understanding**. But to exist **in reality as well** is greater than to exist in the understanding alone. If that being existed only in the understanding, we could think of a greater one, namely a being that also exists in reality: this contradicts the definition. Hence the being than which nothing greater can be thought exists in reality. Anselm adds, in a second form, that such a being cannot be thought not to exist, since **necessary** existence is greater than contingent existence.
- *Its merits.* The definition fits the idea of God as the supreme perfection that believers and many philosophers share. The argument has a clear logical structure (a reductio ad absurdum), and for Anselm it expresses faith seeking understanding: the believer already believes and seeks to see why it is necessarily so.
- *Later supporters.* **Descartes** gave a version based on the idea of a supremely perfect being whose perfections include existence, and **Leibniz** held it valid provided that the concept of such a being is shown to be possible. In the twentieth century, modal versions defended by Plantinga revived it.

**Antithesis: the assertion does not prove God's existence.**

- *Gaunilo*, a contemporary monk, objected that the same reasoning would prove the existence of a "perfect island" than which none greater can be thought, which is absurd. Anselm answered that the argument applies only to a being whose greatness is not limited by any degree, but the objection is still held to show that existence cannot be drawn from a definition alone.
- **Aquinas** rejected the argument as a proof for us: the existence of God may be self-evident in itself, but it is not self-evident to us, who do not know God's essence, and he preferred proofs starting from the world.
- **Hume** held that whatever we can conceive as existing we can also conceive as not existing, so no being exists by necessity of its concept; and **Kant** argued that **existence is not a real predicate**: adding "exists" to the concept of a thing does not add a property to it (a hundred imagined coins contain no fewer coins than a hundred real ones), so the move from "greater if existing" to "exists" is illegitimate.
- *Further doubts*: the argument assumes that the concept is coherent and that "greater" can be measured on a single scale; and the believer who already accepts the premises is not constrained to accept a conclusion that non-believers refuse.

**Synthesis.** The assertion is better understood as an **analysis of the concept of God and a statement of faith** than as a compelling demonstration. The definition has lasting value: it states what believers mean by God, the supreme being, and shows that the idea of God, if coherent, is that of a necessary being. But the step from the idea to the reality needs an additional premise (that existence is a perfection, or that the concept is possible) which the critics have good reasons to challenge. The argument also remains instructive in showing the limits of reasoning from definitions.

**Conclusion.** Anselm's formula is a profound definition of God and a **valid piece of reasoning from its own premises**, but most philosophers judge it **unconvincing as a proof**, mainly because of the objections of Kant and Hume to treating existence as a perfection that can be derived from a concept. Its strength lies in clarifying the concept of God and in provoking some of the deepest discussions in the philosophy of religion.
